overview: This eastern Libyan region combined Mediterranean towns, pastoral communities and the Sanusi religious network. The map’s 1715 to 1878 interval covers Ottoman and Karamanli rule; it does not represent one independent kingdom or the much earlier Greek city of Cyrene.

periods.title: Karamanli provincial rule
periods.summary: Rulers based in Tripoli exercised uneven authority over eastern Libya and its local leaders.

periods.title: Ottoman posts and Sanusi lodges
periods.summary: Direct Ottoman rule returned in 1835; the Sanusi network developed alongside imperial administration.

items.text: Before permanent inland posts, Karamanli officials worked through tribal leaders responsible for order and taxation. Their authority followed communities more than a neatly bounded district with a government office in its center.

Ottoman forts at Al-Marj and Al-Qayqab were built in 1851 to 1852 along the inland Benghazi-to-Derna road. Surviving structures and local testimony helped geographer Xavier de Planhol reconstruct this expanding administrative network.

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi founded the Bayda lodge in 1843. His movement joined religious teaching to practical organization; lodges became places where worshippers, learners and traveling merchants could meet.

By the mid-nineteenth century, lodges linked caravan routes, coastal inlets and older settlement sites. Religious communities provided education and work, while tolls, gifts and trade helped sustain the network.

Visiting Benghazi in 1852, James Hamilton described courtyard houses roofed with juniper trunks, mats and plaster. Drinking water arrived in skins or barrels from outside wells; courtyard wells supplied brackish water.
Hamilton also reported a Benghazi doctor supervising street cleaning and inspecting meat before sale. Public health involved markets and streets as well as sickbeds.

In Derna, Hamilton saw streams divided into channels through the town, with water distributed to gardens at regular times. Palms, bananas and vines grew around houses: the watering schedule mattered to everybody downstream.

Near Cyrene, Hamilton witnessed someone buying half a mare: shared ownership, rather than a spectacularly unwise veterinary operation. The buyer cared for her, and the owners shared her foals under an agreed arrangement.

The Sanusi founder’s first teacher was his aunt, Sayyida Fatima, in Algeria. Later, at Jaghbub, he assembled a library including law, literature, history and astronomy. His own education reminds us that learned women also shaped this intellectual world.

A small Arabic sample is “المسائل العشر”, meaning “The ten questions”, from the cataloged title of al-Sanusi’s religious work. The cited Cairo printing dates to 1353 AH, or 1934/35; the author died in 1859, so this is a later edition of nineteenth-century scholarship.

Cyrenaica’s trade reached far beyond its coast: barley went to England, cattle to Malta and Izmir, wool to Genoa and Marseilles, and butter to Istanbul. Everyday farm products tied households to Mediterranean markets.

Caravan commerce also carried ivory, skins, salt and ostrich feathers. It included enslaved people, and the trade persisted despite an Ottoman prohibition in 1857. Those routes brought both livelihoods and devastating coercion.

ending.text: The map stopping in 1878 is not a historical collapse. Ottoman rule continued until the Italian invasion of 1911 and the 1912 settlement; local resistance continued beyond that transfer of imperial claims.
